passages.title: The Book is truly from the Lord
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the surah's opening claim about itself: this Book has come down from the Lord of all that exists, there is no room for doubt about that, and the accusation that Muhammad ﷺ invented it is simply false. What holds the three together is a single movement — three letters, then a declaration, then the answer to an objection — ending in the reason the Book was sent at all: to warn a people to whom no warner had come, so that they might be guided. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it at the close of its comment, all three verses together carry "an affirmation of the veracity of the Qur'an and the Prophet of Islam."

## A surah the Prophet ﷺ kept returning to

The passage opens with three Arabic letters recited one by one: *alif*, *lām*, *mīm*. Ibn Kathir does not expound them here; he says plainly that he discussed the individual letters at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah and that there is no need to repeat that here. That restraint is itself instructive. These openings are not treated as a puzzle to be forced; the commentator states what he has to say once and moves on to what the passage is arguing.

What the sources do show is how deeply these opening words were woven into the Prophet's ﷺ own practice — so much so that the surah is identified by them. Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Virtues of Surah Alif Lam Mim As-Sajdah," and in the reports themselves the surah is named by its first words, *Alif Lām Mīm — Tanzīl*: "Alif Lam Mim. The revelation of…"

**In the Fajr prayer of Friday.** In the Book of the Friday prayer, al-Bukhari recorded that Abu Hurayrah said the Prophet ﷺ used to recite in Fajr on Fridays *Alif Lām Mīm — Tanzīl* (this surah, as-Sajdah) and "Has there not been over man…" — Sūrat al-Insān. Ibn Kathir notes that this was also recorded by Muslim.

**Every night before sleeping.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Jabir said the Prophet ﷺ would never sleep until he recited *Alif Lām Mīm — Tanzīl* (as-Sajdah) and "Blessed be He in Whose Hand is the dominion" — Sūrat al-Mulk.

So this is a surah he returned to weekly at the most public moment of the Muslim week, and nightly at the most private. Before a single word of the argument has been unpacked, that is already worth carrying away: these words were on his tongue at both ends of his life's rhythm.

## Where the "no doubt" actually falls

**تَنزِيلُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ لَا رَيۡبَ فِيهِ مِن رَّبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ** — "The revelation of the Book in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of all that exists."

Ibn Kathir gives this section the heading "The Qur'an is the Book of Allah in which there is no Doubt." Then notice carefully how he reads the phrase *lā rayba fīhi*, "no doubt in it." He does not simply say the Book contains nothing doubtful. He explains: **"there is no doubt whatsoever that it has been revealed… from the Lord of all that exists."** On this reading, the denial of doubt is not floating loose over the contents of the Book — it attaches precisely to the claim of origin. The question on the table was never whether the Qur'an was beautiful or coherent; it was *where it came from*. Ibn Kathir hears the ayah answering exactly that question: about the source, there is nothing to hesitate over.

And the source is named as *Rabb al-ʿālamīn* — "the Lord of all that exists." Not "your Lord" yet, not the Lord of one people. A Book from such a Lord cannot be a local or tribal document; its authority is as wide as His lordship. Hold that phrase, because within a few words the passage will change it.

## The accusation, and the answer that is not a debate

**أَمۡ يَقُولُونَ ٱفۡتَرَىٰهُ** — "Or say they: 'He has fabricated it?'"

Having stated the truth, Allah now turns, in Ibn Kathir's words, to tell us about the idolators. Ibn Kathir spells out precisely what the charge amounted to: **"they say, he has fabricated it, i.e., he has made it up by himself."** That is the entire accusation, and it is worth seeing how small it is once stated flatly. They did not deny that the words were extraordinary. They proposed a different author.

**بَلۡ هُوَ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ** — "Nay, it is the truth from your Lord."

The answer is not an argument constructed against them. It is a re-assertion of what was already said — sharpened by a change of pronoun. A moment earlier the Book came from "the Lord of all that exists." Here it is "from **your** Lord," addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ, who was carrying the accusation personally. The same Lord of all that exists is his own Lord, standing behind him. Being called a liar by your own people is met not with a debate but with the reminder of Who sent you.

**And then, immediately, the purpose.** The ayah continues: **لِتُنذِرَ قَوۡمًا مَّآ أَتَاهُم مِّن نَّذِيرٍ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ** — "so that you may warn a people to whom no warner has come before you" — **لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَهۡتَدُونَ** — "in order that they may be guided." Ibn Kathir glosses that closing phrase simply: it means **"in order that they may follow the truth."** Guidance here is not an inner glow; it is arriving at the truth and going along with it. Note the sequence: the *warning* is the means, the *guidance* is the goal. The severity is in service of mercy. Even the accusation of forgery is answered by returning to the purpose — their own rescue.

So the three verses move as one arc: the letters, the declaration of origin, the objection, the restatement, and the reason the whole thing was sent down. Everything in the passage bends toward that last clause.

## "A people to whom no warner has come": the difficulty and its resolution

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does its most careful work on the passage, because the closing clause raises a real question. Elsewhere the Qur'an says: **وَإِن مِّنْ أُمَّةٍ إِلَّا خَلَا فِيهَا نَذِيرٌ** — "And there was no community without a warner having passed among them" (35:24). If every community has had a warner, how can these Arabs be a people to whom no warner came?

**The answer lies in the word *nadhīr*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in our ayah, *nadhīr* ("warner") means a *rasūl* — a messenger. The sense is that no messenger had appeared amidst the Quraysh of Makkah before the Prophet ﷺ. This does not mean the call of the messengers had never reached them. In 35:24, by contrast, the word *nadhīr* appears **in its general lexical sense** — that is, in its ordinary dictionary meaning: anyone who calls people towards Allah, "whether a messenger or prophet or one of their deputies, khalīfah or the ʿālim of dīn," that is, a scholar of the religion carrying the prophetic legacy forward.

So the two verses speak about two different things. From 35:24, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it seems that the call of pure monotheism (*tawhīd*) had reached all communities and groups — and this is "certainly the dictate of universal Divine mercy." But it need not have reached them through a prophet standing among them in person.

**Abu Hayyan's principle.** The commentator Abu Hayyan is cited for a striking observation: the call to *tawhīd* and *īmān* has never ceased in any time or place or people. And wherever a long time passed after the appearance of a prophet, it resulted in a dearth of those having the knowledge of the legacy of prophethood — and thereupon some new prophet or messenger was sent. This requires that the call to tawhīd should certainly have reached the Arab peoples, and much earlier. But it is not necessary that it was brought by a prophet or messenger in person; it is possible that it reached them through the learned, serving as deputies to the prophetic mission.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore concludes that the verses of this surah, of Sūrah Yā Sīn, and others which state that no *nadhīr* had appeared amidst the Quraysh before the Prophet ﷺ must be approached with this consideration: *nadhīr* there means a prophet and messenger in the technical sense — no prophet or messenger had come amidst those people — even though the call to tawhīd and faith may have reached them through other means.

## The lone monotheists of the *fatrah*

There is a beautiful corollary to this, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it. Before the period called the *fatrah* — the interval before the appearance of the Prophet ﷺ — it stands proved about some blessed souls that they firmly adhered to the faith of Sayyidna Ibrahim and Ismaʿil (peace be upon them): they believed in the Oneness of Allah and were averse to the worship of idols and to sacrifices for them.

**Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl.** Rūh ul-Maʿānī reports from the *Maghāzī* of Musa ibn ʿUqbah about one such man. Zayd had met the Prophet ﷺ before he was ordained as a prophet, but died before the prophethood began — in the year the Quraysh had built the edifice of the Baytullah, five years before the prophethood. About him, Musa ibn ʿUqbah says: "He used to stop the Quraish from indulging in the worship of idols. He opposed the offering of sacrifices in the name of idols as an evil practice and would not eat the meat from animals slaughtered by the Mushriks." A man alone in a city of idols, refusing even the meat.

His son, Saʿid ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr — one of the celebrated ten among the noble Sahabah — is reported by Abu Dawud Tayalisi to have submitted before the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "You already know about my father that he adhered to pure monotheism and rejected idolatry. Can I, then, pray for his forgiveness?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes, for him the prayer of forgiveness is permissible. He will, on the day of Qiyamah, rise as a community of his own." (This is reported via Rūh ul-Maʿānī.) One man, counted as an *ummah*. What a thing to be said of someone who stood alone.

**Warqah ibn Nawfal.** Likewise Warqah ibn Nawfal, who was present during the initial period of the prophethood and the revelation of the Qur'an, was an adherent of pure monotheism. He had expressed his resolve to help the Prophet ﷺ, but he died soon after.

These examples, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, prove that the people of Arabia were not totally deprived of the Divine call to faith and monotheism; it is only that no prophet had appeared amidst them as such. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

**Take the origin question seriously, because the passage does.** It does not ask you to feel that the Qur'an is inspiring; Ibn Kathir locates the "no doubt" at the point of its having been revealed from the Lord of all that exists. Your relationship with the Book stands or falls there.

**The accusation has never gone out of circulation.** "He made it up himself" — Ibn Kathir's plain paraphrase of the charge — is the oldest objection to the Qur'an and still among the commonest. Notice that the Qur'an's own answer is not defensive elaboration but a firm restatement of the truth, anchored in "from your Lord."

**Warning is for the sake of guidance.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *laʿallahum yahtadūn* — "in order that they may follow the truth" — sets the tone for how anyone conveys this message. If warning ever becomes an end in itself rather than a door to guidance, it has drifted from the ayah.

**And there is comfort in the *fatrah*.** Zayd ibn ʿAmr had no prophet among his people and no congregation to stand in — and he still refused the idols, and was told he would rise as a community of his own. If a believer today feels isolated in holding to tawhīd, this passage's own commentary answers them.

passages.title: Dominion with no protector beside Him
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The sūrah has just affirmed the truth of the Qur'an and of the Prophet ﷺ sent with it — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes of the opening verses, "All three verses cited above carry an affirmation of the veracity of the Qur'an and the Prophet of Islam." These three ayat now answer the question that lies underneath that claim: who is the Lord who sent it? The answer comes in one unbroken movement — Allah created the heavens and the earth and all between them (ayah 4), Allah directs the command that runs between heaven and earth (ayah 5), and He does so as the Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Almighty, the Most Merciful (ayah 6). Ibn Kathir titles the whole unit in a single phrase: *Allah is the Creator and Controller of the Universe.*

That title is the shape of the passage: **origin**, then **ongoing government**, then **the character of the One who governs**. And in the middle of ayah 4, right after the statement about creation, comes the conclusion the passage is driving at: "You have none, besides Him, as a protector or an intercessor." Creation is not being described for its own sake. It is being described to strip away every rival a person might be leaning on.

## Ayah 4: creation, then the Throne

Ibn Kathir opens plainly: "Allah tells us that He is the Creator of all things. He created the heavens and earth and all that is between them in six days, then He rose over the Throne."

Notice how total the phrasing is. Not merely the heavens, not merely the earth, but "all that is between them" — which leaves nothing outside the sentence. There is no third category of existence that came from somewhere else. Ibn Kathir's own summary is as wide as language allows: He is "the Creator of all things."

**"Then He rose over the Throne" (*thumma istawā ʿalā al-ʿarsh*).** Ibn Kathir's entire comment on this phrase is one clause: "then He rose over the Throne — we have already discussed this matter elsewhere." He refers the reader to a fuller discussion earlier in his tafsir, and that discussion is not part of the material before us. So this commentary will not go past his words: the phrase is affirmed exactly as Allah revealed it, and nothing is added to it here. What the sources in front of us do develop, immediately and at length, is the sovereignty that runs through the rest of the passage — Ibn Kathir's next sentence begins, "only He is the Sovereign Who is in control of all affairs."

## "You have none besides Him as a protector or an intercessor"

**مَا لَكُم مِّن دُونِهِ مِن وَلِيٍّ وَلَا شَفِيعٍ**

Ibn Kathir explains the denial like this: it means "only He is the Sovereign Who is in control of all affairs, the Creator of all things, the Controller of all things, the One Who is able to do all things. There is no Creator besides Him, no intercessor except the one to whom He gives permission."

So the two things being denied — a *walī* (rendered here as a protector) and a *shafīʿ* (an intercessor) — are denied on the strength of what has just been established. If He alone created, alone controls, and alone is able to do all things, then there is simply no one else in the picture to protect you or to plead for you.

That last clause of Ibn Kathir's is precise and worth pausing over: "no intercessor except the one to whom He gives permission." The ayah does not say intercession never happens. It says you have no intercessor *besides Him* — none independent of Him. Intercession exists only where He gives permission for it. The door is therefore not closed on intercession; what is closed is the idea that anyone may be approached instead of Allah, as though they held something over Allah.

**"Will you not then remember?" (*afalā tatadhakkarūn*).** Ibn Kathir tells us exactly who is being addressed: "this is addressed to those who worship others apart from Him and put their trust in others besides Him — exalted and sanctified and glorified be He above having any equal, partner, supporter, rival or peer, there is no true deity or Lord except Him."

Two things are worth noticing. First, he names **worship** and **trust** together as one problem: those who "worship others apart from Him" and those who "put their trust in others besides Him" are addressed in the same breath. Second, the wording of the question is not "will you not learn?" but "will you not *remember*?" — it asks the listener to recall, and what he is asked to recall is what the ayah has just laid in front of him: the heavens, the earth, and everything between them.

Ibn Kathir's list of negations — no equal, no partner, no supporter, no rival, no peer — leaves nothing out. Every way of imagining a second alongside Allah is named and denied.

## Ayah 5: the command that descends and the deeds that ascend

**يُدَبِّرُ ٱلْأَمْرَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ يَعۡرُجُ إِلَيۡهِ**

Ayah 4 established that He made it; ayah 5 shows Him directing it — the second half of Ibn Kathir's title, *Controller of the Universe*. There is movement in two directions here: the command comes **down**, and something goes back **up**.

Ibn Kathir describes the downward reach: "His command comes down from above the heavens to the furthest boundary of the seventh earth." Nothing lies outside that range. He connects it to another ayah: "It is Allah Who has created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof. The command descends between them" (65:12).

And the upward movement: "Deeds are raised up to the place of recording above the lowest heaven." That is what ascends — the record of what His servants do. So the same ayah that describes government of the whole cosmos also quietly places your own actions inside that movement.

**The five hundred years.** Ibn Kathir then gives the scale involved: "The distance between heaven and earth is the distance of five hundred years traveling, and the thickness of the heaven is the distance of five hundred years." And he reports from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak: "The distance covered by the angel when he descends or ascends is the distance of five hundred years, but he covers it in the blink of an eye."

Hold both halves of that together, because the point is in the contrast between them. The distance is one of five hundred years' travelling — and it is crossed in the blink of an eye.

## The day of a thousand years: what the scholars said

**فِى يَوْمٍ كَانَ مِقْدَارُهُۥٓ أَلْفَ سَنَةٍ مِّمَّا تَعُدُّونَ** — "in one Day, the measurement of which is a thousand years of your reckoning."

The two sources before us read this phrase in different directions, and it is worth seeing both rather than flattening them.

**Ibn Kathir** reads it together with the sentence it sits in — the descending command and the ascending deeds — and moves straight from it to the conclusion: "meaning, He is controlling all these affairs. He sees all that His servants do, and all their deeds, major and minor, significant and insignificant, ascend to Him."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** treats it under the heading *The length of the day of Qiyāmah*, setting it beside the verse of Sūrah al-Maʿārij: "in a day the extent of which is fifty thousand years" (70:4). Why one thousand in one place and fifty thousand in another?

Maʿārif gives the explanation that appears in *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*: since that day will be horrendous, people would find it very long, and the length will be felt in terms of one's own measure of faith and deeds — "Big criminals will find the day longer while the small ones will find it comparatively shorter, so much so that the day some would feel to be of a thousand years, to others, it would appear as of fifty thousand years."

But Maʿārif does not let that settle the matter. It notes that *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī* reports several other explanations from the ʿUlamāʼ and the Sufiyāʼ, and then says of them plainly: "all these are nothing but conjectures. Something which can be traced back to a proved meaning of the Qur'an or something which can be believed in is just not there."

**The soundest road, and the dignity of "I do not know."** Maʿārif concludes that the most sound approach here is the one taken by the early elders of Islam, the Ṣaḥābah and the Tābiʿīn: "They had left the knowledge of this difference of one and fifty to Allah without explaining it on the basis of human whims and, on their part, they had found it sufficient to say, 'we do not know.'" It cites ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him:

> "They are two days mentioned by Allah Taʿālā in His Book. Allah Taʿālā knows best about them and I dislike to say in the matter of the Book of Allah that which I do not know."

There is a whole discipline of faith in that sentence. A Companion declined to speak about two verses whose explanation he had not been given, and treated saying about the Book of Allah what he did not know as something to be *disliked* — not merely risky. If he held back there, a reader who feels the urge to have every cosmic detail resolved can afford to hold back too.

## Ayah 6: the names that close the passage

**ذَٰلِكَ عَـٰلِمُ ٱلْغَيْبِ وَٱلشَّهَـٰدَةِ ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ**

"That is He" — the demonstrative points back at everything just described: the One who created the heavens and the earth and all between them, who rose over the Throne, besides whom there is no protector and no intercessor, whose command descends and to whom deeds ascend. *That* is who this is. And He is named three ways.

**All-Knower of the unseen and the seen.** Ibn Kathir ties this name straight to the governing just described: "meaning, He is controlling all these affairs. He sees all that His servants do, and all their deeds, major and minor, significant and insignificant, ascend to Him." Control of that kind and knowledge of that kind are one subject in his comment, not two.

**al-ʿAzīz, al-Raḥīm — the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.** Ibn Kathir's comment on the pairing is among the most beautiful lines in his treatment of this sūrah: "He is the Almighty Who has subjugated all things to His control, and to Whom everybody submits, and He is Most Merciful to His believing servants. He is Almighty in His mercy and Most Merciful in His might. This is perfection: might combined with mercy and mercy combined with might, for He is Merciful without any hint of weakness."

Note the last clause especially — "Merciful without any hint of weakness." His mercy is never to be mistaken for an inability to act, and Ibn Kathir does not present the two names as pulling against each other but as one perfection: might in the mercy, mercy in the might.

## Living it

**Audit what you are treating as a protector.** Ibn Kathir says the question addresses those who "worship others apart from Him **and put their trust in others besides Him**" — worship and trust in the same sentence. A job, a savings account, a relative with influence, a reputation: the moment the heart quietly settles on one of these as the thing that will actually keep it safe, this ayah is speaking to it. The response is not to abandon means, but to stop mistaking a means for a protector when "only He is the Sovereign Who is in control of all affairs."

**Give up the search for leverage.** There is "no intercessor except the one to whom He gives permission." So there is no route that goes around Allah, no one to be approached instead of Him. That is not a loss: it leaves you dealing directly with the One whom this very passage names *ar-Raḥīm*. Ask Him.

**Remember that your deeds are travelling upward.** "Deeds are raised up to the place of recording," and He sees "all their deeds, major and minor, significant and insignificant." Nothing you did today was too small to be carried up and too small to be seen — a warning about the hidden sin, and a consolation about the unnoticed good.

**Let the unanswered stay unanswered.** Follow Ibn ʿAbbās. Where the Qur'an mentions something whose explanation has not been given, the mature answer is that Allah knows best about it — and a guess is not to be dressed up as knowledge about the Book of Allah.

**And answer the question the passage asks.** *Afalā tatadhakkarūn* — "Will you not then remember?" The passage does not close by informing you. It closes by naming the One you are dealing with — All-Knower of the unseen and the seen, All-Mighty, Most Merciful — and leaving the question with you.

passages.title: Man shaped from clay, given spirit
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat trace the making of the human being: everything Allah created He created well, and the finest of that making is man — begun from clay, continued from a fluid the ayah itself calls humble, then shaped, then given a breath of spirit and the faculties of hearing, sight and reason. The passage closes on the natural response to all this — gratitude — with the quiet reproach that little of it is actually given.

Ibn Kathir points out where this comes in the surah's flow: when Allah mentions the creation of the heavens and the earth, He follows that by mentioning the creation of man. The eye is lifted to the sky and then turned inward to the body reading the words.

## "Who made everything He has created good" (ayah 7)

The opening phrase is **ٱلَّذِيٓ أَحۡسَنَ كُلَّ شَيۡءٍ خَلَقَهُۥ** — rendered in our translation as "Who has perfected everything He created." Ibn Kathir tells us that Allah has created everything well and formed everything in a goodly fashion, and reports that Malik said, narrating from Zayd bin Aslam, that the phrase means: "He created everything well and in a goodly fashion." Not merely that the products are handsome, but that the workmanship is good — the making itself is sound.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this up. Allah has made whatever He created in this world under the dictate of His wisdom, and under the essential consideration of what is beneficial for the whole system; therefore everything has a beauty of its own. And the most beautiful and better than all, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is the making of man — as Allah says elsewhere, *laqad khalaqnā al-insāna fī aḥsani taqwīm*, "Surely, We did create man in the best of symmetry" (95:4).

**But what about the things we call ugly?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection. There are creations other than man that may outwardly be taken as bad: dogs, pigs, snakes, scorpions and wolves are commonly considered bad because they are either poisonous or beastly. But in terms of the expedient benefits of the world as a whole, none of these is really bad. Each has a place in a system whose full workings we do not see. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes a proverbial poetic observation in Urdu: *there is nothing useless in the world; there is no one bad in the workshop of nature.*

The point is pressed further. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the author of Bayan ul-Qur'an, who notes that the text's *kulla shay'in* — "whatever" — includes all **substances** and **accidents**: things which have corporeal substance, such as animals, plants and minerals, as well as incorporeal things, which include even morals and deeds. So much so that morals which are identified as bad — anger, greed, desire and their likes — are not bad in themselves. The bad about them emerges when they are used out of place. If they stay in their proper place, there is nothing bad in them at all.

So the sense being driven home in the ayah relates to the objective of the creation of these things — *takwīn*, their bringing into being and introduction into the world — and that, according to divine wisdom, is nothing but good. The qualities "good" and "bad" attach at a second level: in relation to human acts and their effects on individuals — what Bayan ul-Qur'an calls one's right or choice employed in doing something. And there the necessary qualification is added, so that no one twists the ayah into "everything is fine": in those terms, everything is *not* good. It is circumscribed by a little detail, and the detail is small and clear — whatever Allah has not allowed is not good, but is rather bad. Then, as the scholars do at the edge of such discussions, the passage ends: *Allah knows best.*

This reframes how a believer looks at the world. Nothing in creation is a design flaw. What we call evil, on this reading, is a good thing used out of its place — outside what Allah has allowed. Which puts the responsibility exactly where the rest of the passage is about to put it: on the creature who was given faculties and told to be grateful.

## From clay to a humble fluid (ayat 7–8)

**"And He began the creation of man from clay."** Ibn Kathir is brief and precise: this means He created the father of mankind, Adam, from clay.

**"Then He made his descendants from an extract of a humble fluid."** Ibn Kathir explains this as describing how humanity reproduces from that point on: they reproduce in this fashion, from a *nutfah* — a drop — which comes from the loins of men and from between the ribs of women.

Notice what the Qur'an does not do. It does not dignify the ingredients. Clay is common earth; the fluid is called humble — Ibn Kathir's rendering has it as "despised water." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly this, and it is the heart of the passage: the making of man as the most superior form of creation was **not** because the essential ingredient of his creation was most noble, elegant and superior, as though the honour were already latent in the substance. In fact, the essential ingredient that went into his making was something as mean and lowly as the semen. Thereafter, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the rest was a masterpiece of Allah's perfect power and profound wisdom. It was this great combination that took something so low to such a height that man was rated as the most noble Divine creation.

This is why the two claims of the passage need each other. Ayah 7 says Allah made everything *well*; ayat 7–8 tell us He did it starting from clay and a humble fluid. Take either away and you lose the force of it. The excellence on display, on Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading, is testimony to the power and wisdom of the Maker — and leaves the creature nothing to boast of in the raw material.

## The shaping and the breath (ayah 9)

**"Then He fashioned him in due proportion."** Ibn Kathir explains this of Adam: when He created him from clay, He created him and gave him shape and made him upright. The clay does not merely become a body; it becomes a body standing upright, shaped, finished.

**"And He breathed into him of His spirit."** Ibn Kathir renders this simply: He breathed into him the soul. Our translation puts the phrase as "had a spirit of His Own ˹creation˺ breathed into" him. That breath is the boundary between a formed shape and a living person. What the ayah gives us is the fact of it, and Ibn Kathir's gloss keeps to what is given — the soul. Beyond that the wording does not invite us into anatomy, and it is enough to know that your life comes from Him.

**"And He gave you hearing, sight and the sense of deduction."** Notice that the wording turns. The ayah has been speaking about *him* — Adam, his offspring, his shaping — and then, mid-sentence, the address is to *you*: **wa jaʿala lakum**, "and He gave *you*." The three faculties named are *al-samʿ* (hearing), *al-abṣār* (sight) and *al-af'idah* — that last word Ibn Kathir explains as the sense of deduction, that is, **reason**.

## "Little is the thanks you give"

The passage lands on a reproach, gently phrased and hard to escape: *qalīlan mā tashkurūn*. Ibn Kathir explains it exactly — little thanks for these strengths with which Allah has provided you. Not "little thanks" in general, but little thanks *for these*: for hearing, for sight, for the reason that deduces.

And he tells us what real thanks looks like, which keeps this from being vague piety: the one who is truly blessed is the one who uses these faculties to worship and obey his Lord, may He be exalted and glorified. That is the definition of *shukr* the passage works with. Gratitude here is not primarily a feeling or a phrase; it is **use** — and specifically use in the service of the One who gave them. That sits naturally alongside the point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gave us at the start: nothing Allah created is bad in itself, and the bad emerges when a thing is used out of its place, outside what Allah has allowed. So the ear Allah made well is thanked by what it chooses to listen to. The eye is thanked by what it refuses to look at. The reason is thanked by being spent in obedience to Him.

## Holding the passage whole

Read together, the three ayat move from the widest statement to the most personal. Allah's making is good everywhere (ayah 7). Its most beautiful instance is a creature He began from clay and continued from a humble fluid (ayat 7–8), so that the height reached testifies to His power and wisdom rather than to the material. He shaped that creature and made it upright, breathed into it the soul, and gave hearing, sight and reason (ayah 9). And then, having handed over these strengths, He notes how rarely thanks is given for them.

**What it asks of you today:** look at the two ends of yourself at once. The material — clay and a humble fluid, nothing to be proud of. The gift — shape, soul, hearing, sight, reason, nothing you contributed to. Humility and gratitude are not two separate duties here; they are the same recognition seen from either end. And the way to discharge both, as Ibn Kathir says, is to use these strengths in the worship and obedience of your Lord, may He be exalted and glorified.

passages.title: Deniers of resurrection meet their reckoning
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer a mockery. The idolaters asked how bodies scattered and lost in the earth could ever be created anew; the passage replies not with an argument about dust but by walking them forward through the very journey they were denying — the angel of death already set over them (ayah 11), the return to their Lord, the courtroom where their heads hang low (ayah 12), and the sentence that closes the door (ayat 13–14). What holds the unit together is one word: **the meeting** (*liqāʾ*). They deny the meeting with their Lord in ayah 10; they are told they will be brought back to their Lord in ayah 11; at that meeting in ayah 12 they plead that they now believe the meeting with Him is true; and in ayah 14 they are told to taste the consequence precisely "because of your forgetting the meeting of this Day of yours." Their mockery is answered with an itinerary.

## The objection: "when we are lost in the earth"

Ayah 10 quotes them: *a-idhā ḍalalnā fī l-arḍ* — "When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be created anew?" Ibn Kathir glosses the first half: it means "when our bodies have been scattered and have disintegrated and dispersed in the earth" — not merely buried, but mixed into the soil. And *khalq jadīd*, "created anew," he reads as their real question: "after that, will we come back again?"

Ibn Kathir then makes a fair-minded concession. They thought it unlikely — "and in terms of their own feeble abilities it is indeed unlikely." Their error was one of scale: they measured by their own powers. "But this is not the case with regard to the power of the One Who created them from nothing, Who when He wills a thing merely says to it, 'Be!' and it is."

**The real diagnosis.** Then comes the turn that changes the subject entirely: *bal hum bi-liqāʾi rabbihim kāfirūn* — "Nay, but they deny the meeting with their Lord." Their objection was dressed as a problem about scattered bodies; the ayah names a different problem altogether. What they will not accept is the meeting with their Lord. That is why the reply that follows is not a lecture on bones and dust but a reminder of an appointment already in place.

## The answer: an angel is already set over you

Ayah 11 opens with a command to the Prophet ﷺ — *Qul*, "Say" — and the answer he is given is not "Allah can do it" but something far closer to home. Ibn Kathir's rendering: "The angel of death, who is set over you, will take your souls." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the same words: "The angel of death who has been assigned for you will take you in full."

Maʿārif draws out why this is the right reply. In the previous ayah the deniers of the Qiyamah (the Resurrection) were wondering how they could be brought back to life after dying and becoming dust; here they are told, in effect: *think of your death first.* "Your heedlessness and ignorance make you think that one's death comes all by itself, just like that. This is not how it is." Death is itself "a great manifestation of the perfect power of Allah Taʿālā" — there is a time fixed for it with Allah, and for it "a standing system run through angels." A man who cannot account for how his own soul leaves his body is in no position to declare a second creation impossible.

**Deputed, not independent.** The clause *alladhī wukkila bikum* — "who is set over you," "who has been assigned for you" — presents the angel as one placed over this task by another. He acts because he has been assigned; the reports gathered below say the same thing from every side.

**Singular and plural.** Maʿārif notes that *malak al-mawt* here is in the singular, taking it to mean the angel who is "the master-manager of death throughout the world," and compares another ayah where the plural appears: *alladhīna tatawaffāhumu l-malāʾikah*, "the ones to whom the angels brought death" (16:28). The hint, it says, is that he "does not do this alone. Many angels under him take part in accomplishing this duty." Ibn Kathir says the same from his side: "The angel of death has helpers," and adds that it was reported in the Hadith that his helpers draw out the soul from the rest of the body until it reaches the throat, and then the angel of death takes it.

**Is he a specific individual?** Ibn Kathir says the apparent meaning of the ayah is that the angel of death is a specific personality among the angels, as is also apparent from the Hadith of al-Barāʾ, which he had quoted in his tafsir of Sūrah Ibrāhīm. He adds: "In some reports he (the angel of death) is called ʿIzrāʾīl, which is well known. This is the view of Qatādah and others." Notice the register — Ibn Kathir grounds the *office* in the ayah and in the hadith, and reports the *name* as something transmitted. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān uses the name freely, with the honorific due to a noble angel: Sayyidunā ʿIzrāʾīl, peace be upon him.

**The world as a platter.** Both commentaries transmit an image from Mujāhid, whom Maʿārif calls a tafsir authority. In Ibn Kathir's wording: "The earth is brought together for him and it is like a platter from which he takes whenever he wants." In Maʿārif's: "before the angel of death, the whole world is very much like an open tray before a human being sprinkled in which there are grains and he picks up whichever he wants." Maʿārif adds that the same subject also appears in a *marfūʿ* report — meaning one traceable to the Prophet ﷺ himself — as mentioned by al-Qurṭubī in *At-Tadhkirah*. Hold that image against ayah 10: the deniers say they are *lost* in the earth. In Mujāhid's picture the earth lies open like a tray.

## What the sources add about death

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers several reports here, and each bends the same way: the angel is a servant, not a sovereign.

**"I make it easy on every believer."** According to a hadith, the Prophet ﷺ once saw the angel of death standing behind the head of an Anṣārī Companion on his deathbed, and asked him to make it easy on his companion. The angel of death said, "Rest assured. I make it easy on every believer." He then invited the Prophet ﷺ to consider the number of people living in towns or villages and in forests, mountains or waters: "I see every one of them five times a day, therefore, I am directly acquainted with everyone of them, young or old." And he concluded with the line that anchors everything: "all this I am telling you about is nothing but what happens with the will and command of Allah. Otherwise, if I wanted to take the life of even a mosquito, I do not have the power to do so — unless there comes the very command of Allah Taʿālā that I have to do it." (Maʿārif gives this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here as the commentary has it.)

**A ruling on the angel's knowledge.** Maʿārif records the ruling: the angel of death does not know the time of anyone's death in advance — not until he is ordered to exact the soul of a certain person (deduced by Aḥmad and Ibn Abī ad-Dunyā from Maʿmar, cited via Mazharī). The appointed hour rests with Allah; even the one who carries out the order learns it only when it is given. Which is exactly the point ayah 11 presses against the mockers.

**Do animals die by his hand?** Here the scholars genuinely differed, and Maʿārif attributes both sides rather than settling it. From the hadith above it seems that it is the angel of death who, subject to divine permission, exacts the soul of a mosquito too — and Imām Mālik said this as well, while answering a question. But some other reports show that this exacting of the soul is particular to human beings, because of their nobility and distinction, while animals die under divine will without the medium of the angel (mentioned by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah from al-Qurṭubī). In support of the second view, Maʿārif cites a report from Sayyidunā Anas transmitted by Abū ash-Shaikh, ʿUqailī, Dailamī and others, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that all animals and insects keep glorifying Allah, for that is their life; when the glorification stops, Allah takes their soul — "The death of animals has not been entrusted with the angel of death." Another related hadith is reported from Sayyidunā Ibn ʿUmar (via Mazharī). Two respectable readings; a believer may hold either without faulting the other.

**Why death gets blamed on diseases.** It appears in yet another hadith, Maʿārif relates, that when Allah handed over to Sayyidunā ʿIzrāʾīl, peace be upon him, the charge of managing the death of everyone in the world, he pleaded that the children of Ādam would give him a bad name, so that every time he was remembered he would be dubbed as evil — and the reply was that this had been taken care of "by placing some obvious diseases and causes of death in the world due to which everyone will attribute death to these diseases and causes," so that he would remain safe from their adverse comments (cited from al-Qurṭubī in his *Tafsir* and *At-Tadhkirah*).

**The messengers you keep ignoring.** Imām al-Baghawī reports, on the authority of Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said that all diseases, and things like pain and wound, are the universal message-bearers of death: they remind every human being of his or her death. Then, when the time of death comes, the angel of death turns towards the dying person and addresses him as a servant of his Lord — asking how many notices he has served on him, how many message-bearers he has sent one after the other, and telling him that all those diseases and accidents delivered at his doors were simply to warn him to get ready for death. Now, the angel says, here he stands, after whom no further bearer of a message will come; now the dying man must say yes to the order of his Lord, necessarily, whether willingly or unwillingly (cited via Mazharī). Every fever, every injury, was a letter. Ayah 11 is the last one.

Then ayah 11 closes: *thumma ilā rabbikum turjaʿūn* — "Then you shall be brought to your Lord." Ibn Kathir: this means, on the Day when you are resurrected and brought forth from your graves to receive your reward or punishment. The mockers said they were lost in the earth. The ayah answers that the grave is a stage on the way, not the end of the road.

## The courtroom: heads bowed (ayah 12)

*Wa-law tarā* — "And if you only could see." Ibn Kathir sets the scene out: Allah tells us the state of the idolaters on the Day of Resurrection and what they will say when they see the Resurrection and are standing before Allah — may He be glorified — humiliated and brought low, *nākisū ruʾūsihim*, with their heads bowed, "i.e., in shame."

Their words are hard to read: *rabbanā abṣarnā wa-samiʿnā* — "Our Lord! We have now seen and heard." Ibn Kathir reads this as: "now we hear what You say and we will obey You." The two faculties are suddenly wide open. He compares 19:38, "How clearly will they see and hear, the Day when they will appear before Us!", and adds that they will blame themselves when they enter the Fire, saying, in 67:10, "Had we but listened or used our intelligence, we would not have been among the dwellers of the blazing Fire!"

So they ask for the one thing that cannot be given: *fa-arjiʿnā naʿmal ṣāliḥan innā mūqinūn* — "so send us back that we will do righteous good deeds. Verily, we now believe with certainty." Ibn Kathir explains that last phrase: "now we are sure and we believe that Your promise is true and that the meeting with You is true." The very *liqāʾ* they denied in ayah 10 is what they now affirm — with the thing itself in front of their eyes.

**Why the request is refused.** Ibn Kathir gives the reason plainly: "the Lord, may He be exalted, knows that if He were to send them back to this world, they would behave as they did previously, and they would reject and disbelieve in the signs of Allah and would go against His Messengers." He cites 6:27, where they are held over the Fire and say, "Would that we were but sent back! Then we would not deny the Ayat of our Lord." Their promise is urgent in the moment and false in substance — and the One who refuses it is the One who knows what they would in fact do. The refusal is not stinginess; it is knowledge.

## The Word that took effect (ayah 13)

*Wa-law shiʾnā la-ātaynā kulla nafsin hudāhā* — "And if We had willed, surely We would have given every person his guidance." Ibn Kathir pairs this with 10:99, "And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together." Allah's power to bring every soul to guidance is not in question for a moment; the passage renders the fantasy of ayah 12 pointless from the start. If guidance imposed on all had been the decree, no return trip would have been required to secure it.

*Wa-lākin ḥaqqa l-qawlu minnī* — "but the Word from Me took effect": *la-amlaʾanna jahannama mina l-jinnati wa-n-nāsi ajmaʿīn*, "that I will fill Hell with Jinn and mankind together." Ibn Kathir: from both classes, "so their abode will be Hell and they will have no escape from it and no way out." He does not linger; he prays: "We seek refuge with Allah and in His perfect Words from that." That reflex is part of the tafsir. The right response to reading about the Fire is not analysis but flight to Allah.

## "Taste it" (ayah 14)

The passage ends with a sentence spoken to the people of the Fire: *fa-dhūqū bi-mā nasītum liqāʾa yawmikum hādhā* — "Then taste because of your forgetting the meeting of this Day of yours." Ibn Kathir says this is said to them by way of rebuke: "taste this punishment because you denied it and believed that it would never happen; you tried to forget about it and acted as if you had forgotten it." Note the precision in his gloss — the "forgetting" was not an innocent lapse of memory but a denial lived out, acting as though the Day were not coming.

**"Surely, We too will forget you."** This is the most delicate phrase in the passage, and Ibn Kathir explains it while guarding it: the meaning is "We will deal with you as if We have forgotten you," and he states the safeguard outright — "but nothing escapes Allah's attention." Read together, those two sentences leave no room for imagining any lapse in Allah's knowledge; what the abandoned will experience is being dealt with as the forgotten are dealt with. And it is measured: "He makes the punishment fit the crime," forgetting answered with forgetting. He cites 45:34: "This Day We will forget you as you forgot the meeting of this Day of yours."

Then: *wa-dhūqū ʿadhāba l-khuldi bi-mā kuntum taʿmalūn* — "so taste you the abiding torment for what you used to do." Ibn Kathir: because of your disbelief and rejection. And he closes with 78:24–25 — "Nothing cool shall they taste therein, nor any drink. Except Hamim, and Ghassaq" (he leaves those two words untranslated) — running on to 78:30, "No increase shall We give you, except in torment." The verb "taste" that opened the ayah is picked up there and turned bitter.

## Living it

The mockery of ayah 10 and the forgetting of ayah 14 are not the same sin, and the second is the one within our reach.

**Take your own death as the proof.** Maʿārif's move is the practical heart of this passage: you do not need a philosophy of resurrection so much as an honest look at one death — that a time for it is fixed with Allah, that it comes through a standing system run through angels, and that no one involved in it, angel included, has power over so much as a mosquito's life without the command of Allah.

**Read your illnesses as post.** If pain and sickness are message-bearers of death, as al-Baghawī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās has it, then the honest response to a diagnosis or an injury is not only treatment but preparation. Nobody wants the angel's rebuke about unopened letters.

**Do now what they will beg to be sent back to do.** They ask in ayah 12 for exactly what you have this afternoon: a world where seeing and hearing are still yours to use and righteous deeds are still possible. Ibn Kathir's comment is the sharpest test of all — they would behave as they did previously if returned. The proof that we are not of them is not our confidence about the Hereafter; it is what we do with the time we are still given.

**Do not "forget" the meeting.** The word Allah uses for their crime in ayah 14 is forgetting — living as though the meeting were not coming. The cure is to put it back in view: to speak of it, prepare for it, and pray as Ibn Kathir prayed, seeking refuge with Allah and in His perfect Words from that.

passages.title: The true believers who rise at night
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a portrait of the true believer — drawn not from what he claims but from what his body does: he goes down in prostration when reminded, he lifts his side off the bed at night to call on his Lord, and he gives away what he was given. The passage then ends by refusing to describe his reward, because it cannot be described.

Read together, the three run as one continuous description. Ayah 15 opens with a restriction — **only** these people believe — and everything through to the end of ayah 17 is either the description of those people or the reward waiting for them.

## Where this comes in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the setting. In the verses before this, it says, the disbelievers, the mushriks (those who set up partners alongside Allah) and the deniers of the Day of Qiyāmah were warned. Then, from ayah 15, the tone turns completely. Now come, in Maʿārif's words, the special attributes of sincere believers and the high ranks reserved for them. So this passage is placed as a deliberate contrast: there stood those who received a warning; here are the people who fall on their faces the moment they hear a reminder.

## Ayah 15: the test is what you do when you are reminded

Ibn Kathir takes the phrases of ayah 15 in turn.

**"Only those believe in Our Ayāt"** — meaning, he says, those who *accept them as true*. Faith here is not an opinion held loosely; it is the acceptance of Allah's signs and verses as real.

**"who, when they are reminded of them, fall down prostrate"** — Ibn Kathir's gloss is striking: it means *they listen to them and obey them in word and deed*. The prostration is not merely a posture. Hearing turns straight into obedience; the reminder lands and the whole person goes down with it. Notice what the ayah chooses as its test — not how much a person knows, but how he behaves in the moment a reminder reaches him. Everyone gets reminded. The believer's reflex is to go lower.

**"and glorify the praises of their Lord, and they are not proud"** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, they are not too proud to follow those signs and submit to them, unlike the ignorant among the rebellious disbelievers. He puts alongside it Allah's words elsewhere: *"Verily, those who scorn My worship, they will surely enter Hell in humiliation!"* (40:60). Arrogance is presented not as a personality flaw but as the thing that blocks faith outright.

## Ayah 16: sides that will not settle on the bed

The Arabic of the next description is *tatajāfā junūbuhum ʿan al-maḍājiʿ* — rendered "their sides forsake their beds," and in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "their sides remain apart from their beds." Either way, the picture is physical and intimate: the side of the body lifting away from the bedding, the place where a person is at his most comfortable and most unobserved. The ayah does not simply say "they pray at night." It shows you a body that will not stay lying down.

Ibn Kathir explains it as praying the voluntary night prayer, foregoing sleep and the rest of a comfortable bed. He reports that **Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan** said the ayah refers to the voluntary night prayer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is the position of the majority of commentators — the leaving of the beds and the turning to dhikr and duʿāʾ means the prayer of **Tahajjud** and **nawāfil** offered after rising from sleep (that is, optional prayers, prayed after one has actually slept and then got up) — and names **al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Mālik and al-Awzāʿī** for it. It is supported, Maʿārif notes, by narrations of hadith as well.

But the ayah was read more widely than that, and the range is worth knowing:

- **aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk**, as Ibn Kathir reports, said it refers to ʿIshāʾ prayer in congregation and Fajr prayer in congregation. Maʿārif attributes the same view to **Abū ad-Dardāʾ, Qatādah and Ḍaḥḥāk** — those who pray ʿIshāʾ with the congregation and then go on to pray Fajr with the congregation.
- Maʿārif cites a narration of **Anas**, appearing in Tirmidhī with sound chains of authority, that this ayah was revealed about people who do not sleep before ʿIshāʾ but stay awake waiting for the congregation of ʿIshāʾ.
- Some other reports (Maʿārif, from Muḥammad Ibn Naṣr) apply it to those who offer optional prayers between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** said that people who remember Allah on waking — lying down, sitting, on their sides — are also included in it.

Ibn Kathir and other authorities of tafsīr, Maʿārif reports, held that **there is no contradiction between any of these**. The correct approach is that the ayah is inclusive of them all, while the late-night prayer remains the highest of them; Bayān ul-Qurʼān took the same view.

This is a generous door, and worth pausing on. A believer who cannot yet manage Tahajjud but who guards ʿIshāʾ and Fajr in congregation, or who sits after waking with Allah's name on his tongue, is not outside the ayah — he is standing at its edge. And the summit of it is still there to climb.

## "Calling their Lord in fear and hope"

The word in the ayah is *yadʿūna* — rendered "to invoke their Lord" in Ibn Kathir's translation and "they call their Lord" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. Maʿārif describes what these people are busy with once they rise as dhikr and duʿāʾ — remembrance and supplication, spoken in submission. Night worship is portrayed here as asking, pleading, needing.

And it comes with two wings. Ibn Kathir: in fear of His punishment and in hope of His reward. Maʿārif fills in the inner state: they are apprehensive of His displeasure and punishment while remaining hopeful of His mercy and reward, and it is precisely this combination of fear and hope that keeps them returning to dhikr and duʿāʾ again and again — anxious and animated at the same time. Neither wing alone would get a person out of bed. Fear without hope would break him; hope without fear would let him sleep.

## "And they spend out of what We have bestowed on them"

The wording quietly settles the matter of ownership: what they give away is what *We* provided. Ibn Kathir reads the whole description together as meaning that such people do both the obligatory and the supererogatory acts of worship — the night prayer and the giving are of one piece, secret worship and open generosity — and he adds that their leader in this, in this world and the Hereafter, is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

## From the Sunnah: Muʿādh's question on the road

Ibn Kathir brings a long hadith here that the Prophet ﷺ himself sealed to this very ayah. **Imam Aḥmad recorded** that **Muʿādh bin Jabal** said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey one morning, walking near him. I said, 'O Prophet of Allah, tell me of a deed that will grant me admittance to Paradise and keep me away from Hell.'"

The Prophet ﷺ answered: *"You have asked about something great, and it is easy for the one for whom Allah makes it easy. Worship Allah and do not associate anything with Him, establish regular prayer, pay Zakāh, fast Ramadan and perform pilgrimage to the House."*

Then he said: *"Shall I not tell you of the gates of goodness? Fasting is a shield, charity wipes out sin, and the prayer of a man in the depths of the night."* And then he recited **"Their sides forsake their beds…"** on to **"as a reward for what they used to do"** — our ayah 16 through to the end of ayah 17.

That is the single most useful thing in the whole passage: the Prophet ﷺ recited these two ayat as the commentary on the night prayer, in answer to a man who had asked how to reach Paradise and escape the Fire.

The conversation did not stop there. He asked Muʿādh, *"Shall I not tell you of the greatest of all things and its pillars and pinnacle?"* — "Of course, O Messenger of Allah." He said: *"The greatest of all things is Islam, its pillars are the prayers and its pinnacle is Jihād for the sake of Allah."* Then: *"Shall I not tell you the factor on which all of that depends?"* — "Of course." He took hold of his own tongue and said, *"Restrain this."* Muʿādh said, "O Messenger of Allah, will we be accountable for what we say?" He answered: *"May your mother be bereft of you, O Muʿādh! Will the people be thrown into Hell – (or he said) on their faces – except because of what their tongues say?"*

That "(or he said)" is not a stumble in the telling; it is the transmitters' honesty preserved inside the text. The Arabic of the report as Ibn Kathir gives it keeps both wordings between which the narrator was unsure — *ʿalā wujūhihim*, "on their faces," or *ʿalā manākhirihim*, "on their nostrils" — rather than quietly choosing one. The meaning is not in doubt; only which of the two words the Prophet ﷺ used. It is worth noticing what kind of care the scholars took with speech that was not their own, in a hadith whose whole point is the danger of the tongue.

Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhī, An-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah** in their Sunans, and that At-Tirmidhī said, "It is Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." Maʿārif cites the same report from the Musnad of Aḥmad, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and others. Read in its own order, the hadith puts the night prayer among the gates of goodness and then, in the same breath, hangs everything on guarding the tongue.

## Ayah 17: a hidden reward for hidden deeds

**"No person knows what is kept hidden for them of delights of eyes."** Ibn Kathir: no one knows the vastness of what Allah has concealed for them of everlasting joy in Paradise, and delights such as no one has ever seen.

Then he offers the insight that ties ayah 17 back to ayah 16 with real precision. Note that the Arabic is passive — *what is kept hidden* for them. Why hidden? **Because they conceal their good deeds, Allah conceals the reward for them** — a fitting reward, one that will suit their deeds. The night prayer is the most hideable worship there is: no congregation sees it, no one can be impressed by it. So the recompense is kept out of sight too, until the day it is uncovered.

Ibn Kathir supports this with **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**, who said: "If people conceal their good deeds, Allah will conceal for them what no eye has seen and what has never crossed the mind of man" — recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

Then the hadith. **Al-Bukhārī** quoted this very ayah and recorded from **Abū Hurayrah** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Allah says: 'I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has never crossed the mind of man.'"* And Abū Hurayrah added: "Recite, if you wish: *No person knows what is kept hidden for them of delights of eyes.*" So the Companion himself read ayah 17 as the Qur'anic proof of that hadith. Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **Muslim and At-Tirmidhī**, and At-Tirmidhī said, "It is Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." Another version in **Al-Bukhārī** adds: *"and no body has ever even imagined of. All that is reserved, besides which, all that you have seen is nothing."*

Ibn Kathir also brings, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"Whoever enters Paradise will enjoy a life of luxury and never feel deprivation, his clothes will never wear out, his youth will never fade. In Paradise there is what no eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, and has never crossed the mind of man."* — recorded by **Muslim**.

This is why the ayah names no fruit, no river, no garment. Any description would shrink it. The verse hands you a sealed container and tells you it is beyond your imagining — and then adds **"as a reward for what they used to do,"** tying that unimaginable gift back to plain, repeated, ordinary acts done in the dark.

## The day they are called out

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, citing Ibn Kathir, a narration of **Sayyidah Asmāʾ bint Yazīd** in which the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah gathers everyone, first to last, a proclaimer whose call the whole creation hears will announce that this day everyone on the plain will find out who is really deserving of honour. Then the proclaiming angel will call out: let those rise whose attribute was *"their sides remain apart from their beds."* At that call these people will stand — and, the narration says, **their number will be small**. Some words of the same narration add that they will be sent to Paradise without reckoning, and that afterwards all the others will stand and face the reckoning. (Maʿārif cites the additional wording from Mazharī.)

## Living it

The passage asks for three things, and they are all within reach.

**Let the reminder move you.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 15 makes the test practical: when a verse of the Qur'an reaches you, does it come out as word and deed, or only as agreement? And guard against the one thing the ayah names as fatal — being too proud to submit.

**Give the night something.** The scholars' breadth in ayah 16 means there is no excuse to do nothing: ʿIshāʾ and Fajr with the congregation, staying awake for ʿIshāʾ rather than sleeping before it, optional prayers between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ, remembering Allah the moment you wake — each of these was held by named authorities to fall inside the verse. And keep the summit in view, because the late-night prayer remains the highest of them. When you rise, *call* on Him — with real fear of His punishment and real hope in His reward, which is what keeps a person coming back night after night.

**Then spend, and keep it quiet.** The giving in ayah 16 sits beside the night prayer as part of the same character. And the logic of ayah 17 is an invitation: hide what you can of your good deeds, and Allah hides your reward — which is exactly where you want it kept.

passages.title: Believer and rebel are never equal
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat settle a question the human heart keeps trying to blur: whether the one who believes and the one who breaks loose from Allah's command will be treated alike in the end. The passage asks it as a question (ayah 18), answers it flatly in the same breath, then spells the answer out in two destinies — Gardens in ayah 19, Fire in ayah 20 — before turning to how Allah deals with the rebel *already, here, in this world* (ayah 21) and naming the worst crime of all: being reminded of Allah's signs and walking away from them (ayah 22). What holds the unit together is a single logic: the two are not equal, and everything that follows is the evidence.

## The question that answers itself

**Ayah 18:** *"Is then he who is a believer like him who is rebellious? Not equal are they."*

The Qur'an poses this as a rhetorical question and then refuses to leave even a moment's room for doubt: *lā yastawūn* — "they are not equal." Notice the shift in the Arabic. The question speaks of individuals — *man kāna mu'minan*, "whoever was a believer," *man kāna fāsiqan*, "whoever was rebellious" — but the denial comes in the plural, *lā yastawūn*, "they are not equal." Two men in the question; two whole classes of humanity in the answer.

Ibn Kathir explains what the equality being denied actually refers to: *"i.e., before Allah on the Day of Resurrection."* Allah, he says, "in His justice and generosity, on the Day of Judgement He will not judge those who believed in His signs and followed His Messengers, in the same way as He will judge those who rebelled, disobeyed Him and rejected the Messengers sent by Allah to them."

That word pairing is worth noticing. Ibn Kathir does not trace the difference in treatment to Allah's justice alone; he writes *"justice and generosity"* — both words, side by side. What the generosity looks like, the passage itself is about to show, in ayah 19.

**Why the question at all?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes what the sūrah has been doing just before this. The earlier ayat carried a warning to the disbelievers, the idolaters and those who denied the Day of Resurrection; then from ayah 15 onwards the sūrah describes the special qualities of the sincere believers and the high ranks kept for them. So by ayah 18 two portraits are already hanging side by side. The question is simply: look at these two — can they possibly end the same?

Ibn Kathir gathers three other places where the Qur'an puts the same question, and it is striking how insistently it recurs:

- *"Or do those who earn evil deeds think that We shall hold them equal with those who believe and do righteous good deeds, in their present life and after their death? Worst is the judgement that they make."* (45:21)
- *"Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous good deeds as corruptors on earth? Or shall We treat those who have Taqwā as the wicked?"* (38:28)
- *"Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of the Paradise…"* (59:20)

The repetition tells us something about us. Ayah 45:21 describes people who actually *think* Allah will hold the two groups equal — so this is a confusion the Qur'an expects human beings to fall into, and it names both "their present life and after their death" as the places where the confusion is answered.

## Two men behind the ayah

Ibn Kathir reports that *"'Aṭā' bin Yasār, As-Suddī and others mentioned that this was revealed concerning 'Alī bin Abī Ṭālib and 'Uqbah bin Abī Muʿīṭ."* One of them the believer of the ayah, the other the rebel — and about these two named men Allah declared that they are not the same and never will be.

So the ayah is not only an abstraction; it was revealed about real, named men. And, as Ibn Kathir puts it, *"Allah has judged between them"* in the very next words — because ayah 19 and ayah 20 are the verdict.

## One word, two destinies

Here is the quiet artistry of the passage. Ayah 19 promises the believers *jannāt al-maʾwā* — "the Gardens of Abode." Ayah 20 says of the rebels *fa-maʾwāhumu n-nār* — "the Fire will be their abode." The same word, *maʾwā*, the place you come home to, the place you finally settle. Both groups get a *maʾwā*. Everything depends on which.

**Ayah 19 — "those who believe and do righteous good deeds."** Ibn Kathir unpacks this as two things joined: *"their hearts believed in the signs of Allah, and they did as the signs of Allah dictate, i.e. righteous good deeds."* Faith is what happened inside; righteous deeds are that same faith working outward. The signs were believed *and* acted upon.

Their reward, *jannāt al-maʾwā*, Ibn Kathir describes as Gardens *"in which there are dwellings and houses and lofty apartments"* — not an open field, but a home with rooms and high chambers.

Then one word, easy to skim past: **nuzulan**. It is often translated "as an entertainment," and Ibn Kathir explains it as *"something to welcome and honor a guest."* Think of what is set before an honoured guest the moment he arrives — the hospitality that says *you are wanted here*. That is the tone in which the believer is received into Paradise. And it is *"for what they used to do"* — the hospitality is not arbitrary; it answers a life.

**Ayah 20 — "as for those who rebel."** Ibn Kathir glosses the *fāsiqūn* here simply as *"those who disobeyed Allah."* And in his opening remarks he had described them more fully as those who *"rebelled, disobeyed Him and rejected the Messengers sent by Allah to them."* Notice what that description joins together: disobedience, and the rejection of the Messengers who brought the command.

Their *maʾwā* is the Fire, and the ayah adds the detail that makes it unbearable: *"every time they wish to get away therefrom, they will be put back thereto."* Ibn Kathir renders it as being thrown back in every time they want to escape, and sets alongside it: *"Every time they seek to get away therefrom, from anguish, they will be driven back therein"* (22:22). The attempt to get out is met, every time, by being returned.

Al-Fuḍayl bin ʿIyāḍ pictured it in words that leave no room for comfort: *"By Allah, their hands will be tied, their feet will be chained, the flames will lift them up and the angels will strike them."*

And then the words spoken over them: *"Taste you the torment of the Fire which you used to deny."* Ibn Kathir notes that this is said *"by way of rebuke and chastisement."* The sting is in the last clause — *which you used to deny*. The very thing they had argued was a fiction is now the thing they are inside of. Note also the verb: *taste*. It is the same verb Allah uses of Himself in the next ayah — *"We will make them taste"* — and it binds ayah 20 and ayah 21 together.

## The nearer punishment (ayah 21)

*"And verily, We will make them taste of the near lighter torment prior to the greater torment, in order that they may return."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *adnā* here is used in the sense of **"nearer"** — and *al-ʿadhāb al-akbar*, "the greater punishment," is the punishment of the Hereafter. So the ayah sets two punishments in order: one that arrives first and is lighter, one that comes later and is immense.

What is the nearer one? Ibn 'Abbās said: *"The near torment means diseases and problems in this world, and the things that happen to its people as a test from Allah to His servants so that they will repent to Him."* Ibn Kathir notes that something similar was narrated from a long roll-call of the early authorities — Ubayy bin Kaʿb, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAlqamah, ʿAṭiyyah, Mujāhid, Qatādah, ʿAbd al-Karīm al-Jazarī and Khuṣayf. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the phrase the same way: the worldly *"diseases, sufferings and calamities"* that Allah lets befall people *"in order to warn them against their sins."*

**The purpose clause changes everything.** The ayah does not end with the punishment; it ends with *laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — "so that they may return." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: the aim is *"to chasten and alert them enough so that they leave off their sins and thus earn their deliverance from the Great Punishment of the Hereafter."* And so it concludes, boldly: *"all these sufferings, accidents, diseases and pains that inflict sinners in the world are nothing but a sort of mercy for them in as much as they help them get out of their heedlessness and save themselves from the punishment of the ʾĀkhirah."*

That is the heart of this passage. A small pain now, sent to spare a person an unendurable pain later, is not cruelty — it is a hand on the shoulder. The illness that stops a man in his tracks, the loss that empties his hands, the shock that finally makes him pray: on this reading, Allah is calling him back while there is still time to come.

**But the door can be refused.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to finish the thought: *"for people who take no lesson even from such unwelcome happenings and fail to turn to Allah, for them, this punishment becomes twofold - first, the cash punishment right here in this world and then, the other being the Great Punishment of the Hereafter."* The nearer punishment is only a mercy if it is *read* as one. Unread, it is simply the first instalment.

## When hardship is not punishment at all

An honest reader will immediately object: prophets and the righteous suffered terribly. Does this ayah make their suffering a punishment?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers directly: *"As for the hardships of many kinds that come upon prophets and men of Allah, that is a separate matter. These hardships are a trial for them and trials are the source through which their ranks are raised."*

And it offers a way to tell the difference — not by looking at the hardship, but at the person inside it. Observe such people even under the stress of calamities and hardships, it says, and *"it will be noticed that they have a kind of peace and tranquility emanating from their trust in Allah."* Then it adds the scholar's honesty: *"And it is Allah who knows best."* Which is the right posture — we are told the principle, not given a licence to diagnose whose suffering is which.

## The greatest wrong of all (ayah 22)

*"And who does more wrong than he who is reminded of the Ayat of his Lord, then turns aside therefrom?"*

This is a question of the same kind as ayah 18 — asked so that the answer can only be *no one*. Ibn Kathir spells it out: *"there is no one who does more wrong than the one whom Allah reminds of His signs and explains them to him clearly, then after that he neglects and ignores them, and turns away from them, forgetting them as if he does not know them."*

Trace the sequence in that sentence, because it is the anatomy of the sin. The signs come. They are made **clear** — the person is not left guessing. Then: he neglects, he ignores, he turns away, and finally he forgets *as if he does not know them*. This is not the wrong of the ignorant. It is the wrong of the informed. The reminder reached him and he chose to be unreached.

Qatādah's comment on this reads like a warning shouted across the centuries: *"Beware of turning away from the remembrance of Allah, for whoever turns away from remembering Him will be the most misguided and the most in need, and the most guilty of sin."* Three superlatives, and the middle one is the one nobody expects — *the most in need*. Turning away from Allah does not make a person independent. It leaves him needier than before.

Then the closing words: *"Verily, We shall exact retribution from the criminals."* Ibn Kathir renders the force of it: *"We shall avenge Ourselves on those who do that in the strongest possible terms."* This is Allah's justice speaking of itself, and we affirm it as He described it, without imagining it as anything like human resentment or revenge and without emptying the words of their weight. What the ayah wants a heart to feel is that this is not a matter to be casual about.

## Retribution that need not wait

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a precise observation about the wording. *Al-mujrimīn*, "the criminals," *"includes all kinds of criminals"* — the term is left general. And *intiqām*, the retribution, is likewise general: *"It may be in the mortal world or in the Hereafter or in both."*

It then notes that from some hadith accounts it appears there are three sins whose punishment is experienced in this world too, before the Hereafter. They are: **(1)** to strive against what is Right and True publicly, with flags and slogans; **(2)** to disobey parents; **(3)** to help someone unjust or oppressive. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives this as reported by Ibn Jarīr from Sayyidnā Muʿādh Ibn Jabal.

Look at the second and third of those. Anyone can be pulled into helping an oppressor, and anyone can wound a parent. The passage that opened by dividing believer from rebel closes with a warning drawn wide enough that no reader can set it aside as being about somebody else.

## Living it

**When something painful comes, ask the question the ayah asks.** *Laʿallahum yarjiʿūn* — "so that they may return." Not "why me," but "what am I being called back from?" On the reading of Ibn 'Abbās and the many early authorities with him, hardship in this world comes as a test *"so that they will repent to Him."* To go through it and change nothing is to receive a summons and never open it.

**Guard the moment of the reminder.** Ayah 22 does not condemn a person for not knowing. It condemns turning away *after* the signs have been explained clearly. So the danger point for a practising believer is the small, familiar act of hearing an ayah, feeling the pull, and going back to what he was doing. Qatādah's warning is aimed exactly there.

**Do not measure by the world's ledger.** Ibn Kathir's citation of 45:21 — that some people imagine Allah will hold them equal — names a real temptation. The believer who sees the defiant prospering and himself struggling is looking at an unfinished account. *Lā yastawūn.* The books close elsewhere.

**And let ayah 19 do its work.** *Nuzulan* — the welcome laid out for an honoured guest, and it is *"for what they used to do"*. The ordinary acts, the ones that feel too small to matter, are what the hospitality answers.

passages.title: Moses' Scripture and the guided leaders
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat turn from the Makkan disbelievers back to an older story: Allah gave Musa a Book, that Book became guidance for a whole nation, and out of that nation Allah raised leaders who guided people by His command. What holds the passage together is a single question — **who deserves to lead in religion, and on what terms?** Ayah 23 grounds the Prophet ﷺ by reminding him he stands in a line that runs back to Musa; ayah 24 states the two qualities that earned the Children of Israel their leadership, and hints at how they lost it; ayah 25 hands the whole tangle of their later disputes over to Allah, who alone will settle it on the Day of Resurrection.

## "So be not in doubt of meeting him"

Ibn Kathir begins simply: Allah is telling us that He gave the Book — the Tawrah — to His servant and Messenger Musa, peace be upon him.

Then comes the phrase that has occupied the commentators: **فَلَا تَكُن فِي مِرْيَةٍ مِّن لِّقَائِهِ** — "so be not you in doubt of meeting him." *Liqāʾ* means meeting, an encounter. The difficulty is the little pronoun at the end — *-hi*, "his/its." Meeting **whom**? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid that "in determining it precisely in the verse, the sayings of commentators differ," and lays out the readings side by side rather than forcing one.

**First reading: no doubt about receiving your own Book.** Here the pronoun is taken to revert to *al-kitāb*, the Book — meaning the Qur'an. The sense becomes: the way Allah gave the Book to Sayyidnā Musa (peace be upon him), you too should entertain no doubt about receiving your Book. Maʿārif notes that similar words are used about the Qur'an elsewhere: *"And indeed you [O Muhammad] do receive the Qur'an"* (An-Naml, 27:6). Maʿārif cites this reading from Bayan ul-Qur'an (Khulasah Tafsir). On this reading the ayah is a reassurance about revelation itself: the process that produced the Tawrah is the same process now unfolding upon you, so do not waver about it.

**Second reading: no doubt that you will meet Musa.** Here the pronoun reverts to Musa (peace be upon him), and the ayah is news — the Prophet ﷺ *will* be meeting him, so let no doubt enter about that.
