Maʿārif reports this tafsir from Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, and observes that a meeting on the night of al-Miʿrāj (the ascent to the heavens) "stands proved on the authority of Sahih Ahadith," and that the meeting on the Day of Qiyāmah is likewise proved.

**Third reading: expect to meet what Musa met.** Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reads it as being about the pattern of a prophet's life: the way Sayyidnā Musa (peace be upon him) was given a Book and was then belied and harassed by his people, the Prophet of Islam ﷺ too should anticipate that he will face similar treatment at the hands of his people. Therefore he should not grieve over the pains inflicted by the disbelievers — he should take that as the blessed practice of the prophets, and endure.

Notice that these readings do not fight each other so much as layer. All three say the same thing to a man under pressure: *you are not an anomaly.* The Book, the rejection, and the eventual honour are all part of a road already travelled.

## The night of Isra'

Ibn Kathir gives the second reading its evidence. Qatādah said this phrase "refers to the Night of Isrāʾ," and then narrated that Abū al-ʿĀliyah ar-Riyāḥī said that "the cousin of your Prophet," meaning Ibn ʿAbbās, told him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that on the night of Isrāʾ he saw Musa bin ʿImrān — a tall, brown-skinned man with curly hair, looking like the men of Shanūʾah; and he saw ʿĪsā, a man of medium stature and ruddy white skin, with lank hair; and he saw Mālik the Keeper of Hell, and the Dajjāl.

*(Ibn Kathir reports this narration through Qatādah from Ibn ʿAbbās without naming a collection, so it is given here as the commentary gives it.)*

Ibn Kathir's point is that among the signs which Allah showed His Messenger ﷺ that night was precisely this: **"so be not you in doubt of meeting him"** — that is, the Prophet ﷺ saw Musa and met with him on the Night of Isrāʾ. The doubt is removed not by argument but by experience. What the ayah promised, the Miʿrāj delivered.

And notice how concrete the report is. The assurance about "meeting him" is answered not with an abstraction but with a face: height, complexion, the texture of the hair. That is how Ibn Kathir presents the fulfilment of the verse.

## A Book that was made into a guide

**وَجَعَلْنَاهُ هُدًى لِّبَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ** — "And We made it a guide to the Children of Israel." Ibn Kathir clarifies the pronoun here without hesitation: *"And We made it"* means the Book which We gave to him. Guidance is not something the Book merely contains; Allah **made** it guidance. He cites the near-identical wording of Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: *"And We gave Musa the Scripture and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel (saying): 'Take none other than Me as Trustee'"* (17:2).

That parallel is worth pausing on. Ibn Kathir's cross-reference shows what a Book "made into guidance" is *for*: it tells a people where to place their ultimate reliance — "Take none other than Me as Trustee."

## Ayah 24: the two conditions of leadership

**وَجَعَلْنَا مِنْهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا لَمَّا صَبَرُوا وَكَانُوا بِآيَاتِنَا يُوقِنُونَ** — "And We appointed leaders from among them who guided (people) under Our command, when they observed patience, and kept firm belief in Our verses."

Three things in the wording carry the weight.

**"We appointed" (wa jaʿalnā).** The leadership is *given*, not seized. The same verb that made the Book a guide makes certain men leaders. Nobody in this ayah appoints himself.

**"Under Our command" (bi-amrinā).** Their guiding is not private opinion dressed as religion. Ibn Kathir glosses it: there were among them leaders who guided others **to the truth by the command of Allah**, calling for goodness, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. A leader in religion is a conduit, and what flows through him is not his own.

**"When they were patient" (lammā ṣabarū).** This is the hinge. Ibn Kathir explains it as *cause*: because they were patient in adhering to the commands of Allah and avoiding what He prohibited, and because they believed in His Messengers and followed what they brought — for that reason there were among them leaders who guided.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out into what it calls the **two conditions for the leader of any people**: two reasons why religious leadership was bestowed on some of the sages of Banī Isrāʾīl — (1) the observance of patience, and (2) the certitude of Divine words.

On the first: in terms of Arabic usage, the sense of *ṣabr* is "very wide and general." Literally it means **to tie, or to be firm**. In this place, Maʿārif says, *ṣabr* means to stay firm on the implementation of the Divine injunctions and to hold one's desiring self in check against infringing what Allah has declared *ḥarām* (unlawful) or *makrūh* (reprehensible). Understood that way, *ṣabr* covers one's obedience to all the injunctions of the Sharīʿah — which Maʿārif calls **pragmatic perfection at its best**: perfection in practice, *ʿamal*.

On the second: *yūqinūn* — they were certain of the Divine words. Maʿārif says this includes both halves of the process: the initial understanding of the sense of the verses, and the certitude that emerges out of that comprehension. This it calls **intellectual perfection at its best**: perfection in knowledge, *ʿilm*.

So the verdict: in the sight of Allah, only those who are perfect both in *ʿilm* (knowledge) and *ʿamal* (practice) are worthy of religious leadership.

## Why patience is mentioned before certainty

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something easy to read past. Usually knowledge precedes practice — you learn, then you do. But here perfection in practice has been made to precede perfection in knowledge. Maʿārif reads this arrangement as "a strong hint": **a knowledge which has no corresponding practice with it is just not credible in the sight of Allah.** The qualification for leadership begins at the point where a man's life obeys what he claims to know.

Maʿārif then quotes a saying of some of the ʿUlamāʾ which Ibn Kathir reports in his tafsir of this verse:

> **بِالصَّبْرِ وَالْيَقِينِ تُنَالُ الْإِمَامَةُ فِي الدِّينِ**
> "One can arrive at the station of leadership in religion only through *ṣabr* (patience) and *yaqīn* (certitude)."

Ibn Kathir adds a sharper edge from the early authorities. On **"when they were patient,"** Qatādah and Sufyān both said: "When they patiently shunned the temptations of this world." This was also the view of al-Ḥasan bin Ṣāliḥ. And Sufyān said plainly: "This is how these people were. A man cannot be an example to be followed unless he shuns the temptation of this world."

That is a demanding standard, and it is deliberately placed. The *ṣabr* that qualifies a man to lead is not only patience under pain — it is patience in refusing what the world offers him. A man still hungry for the world will end up leading people toward it.

## How the leadership was lost

Ibn Kathir does not leave the story at its high point. He continues: **then, when they changed the Words of Allah, twisting and distorting them, they lost that position and their hearts became hard.** They change the words from their places, so they do no righteous deeds and have no correct beliefs.

Read the sequence carefully, because it is the whole moral arc of the passage:

1. A Book is given.
2. Firmness in practice and certainty in knowledge earn leadership.
3. The Book is tampered with.
4. Practice collapses, belief collapses, hearts harden, leadership is withdrawn.

Ibn Kathir underlines how much was entrusted to them by quoting: *"And indeed We gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, and the understanding of the Scripture and its laws, and the prophethood; and provided them with good things, and preferred them above the nations. And We gave them clear proofs in matters"* (45:16–17). Book, legal understanding, prophethood, provision, preference, clear proofs — and still the position was lost once the Book itself was handled dishonestly. Privilege is not protection.

## Ayah 25: the difference that only Allah can settle

**إِنَّ رَبَّكَ هُوَ يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فِيمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَخْتَلِفُونَ** — "Verily, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, concerning that wherein they used to differ." Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and comprehensive: their differing was **with regard to beliefs and actions** — both creed and conduct.

And note who is addressed: it is **"your Lord"** — the same Prophet ﷺ who was told in ayah 23 not to doubt is now told whose case this ultimately is. A community that fractured over the Book it was given will not have its dispute closed by history or by the loudest party. Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection.

## Living it

- **When the truth costs you, remember whose road you are on.** Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's reading of ayah 23 is medicine for anyone discouraged by opposition: mistreatment for the sake of revelation is the blessed practice of the prophets. Take it as such, and endure.
- **Do not chase leadership; earn the qualities and leave the appointing to Allah.** In ayah 24 it is Allah who says *"We appointed."* The believer's work is *ṣabr* and *yaqīn*; position, if it comes, comes from Him.
- **Test your knowledge by your practice, not the reverse.** Maʿārif's point about word order is a personal audit: knowledge with no corresponding practice is not credible in the sight of Allah.
- **Watch your relationship with the world.** Sufyān's standard is uncomfortable but clear — a man cannot be an example to be followed while the world still has a hold on him.
- **Handle the revealed text with fear.** What broke the leadership of the Children of Israel, on Ibn Kathir's account, was changing the Words of Allah and shifting them from their places. Bending a text to suit a desire is the first move in that collapse, and hardness of heart is where it ends.
- **Leave the unresolvable to the Day of Resurrection.** Ayah 25 frees a believer from having to win every religious argument. Say the truth, and trust that your Lord will judge between the disputants Himself.

passages.title: Two signs they refuse to read
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat put two pieces of evidence in front of those who reject the Messengers — the ruins of destroyed nations under their feet, and water arriving at dead ground to bring up food — and then ask, with something close to astonishment, why neither is registering. What holds the passage together is the shape of the questions themselves. Ayah 26 ends *"Would they not then listen?"* and ayah 27 ends *"Will they not then see?"* Two signs, two faculties, both intact, neither used.

## Ayah 26: a ruin is a kind of teacher

The opening words are worth slowing down on. Ibn Kathir renders them: *"Is it not a guidance for them: how many generations We have destroyed before them in whose dwellings they do walk about?"* Notice who is doing the guiding. Not a preacher, not an argument — the destruction itself. The wiping out of earlier peoples is presented as an act of teaching, a sign already delivered, already legible. The question is not "have they been told?" but "has it not guided them?" — which quietly places the failure in the listener, not in the evidence.

Ibn Kathir explains the sense: will these people who deny the Messengers not learn from the nations who came before them, whom Allah destroyed for their rejection of His Messengers and their opposition to the straight path the Messengers brought? And he adds the detail that makes it chilling — **no trace is left of them whatsoever.** He brings a verse to make the silence audible:

> *"Can you find a single one of them or hear even a whisper of them?"* (19:98)

**"In whose dwellings they do walk about."** This is the sharpest edge of the ayah. Ibn Kathir's comment: these disbelievers walk about in the very places where those earlier disbelievers used to live, but they do not see any of the former inhabitants, for they have gone. He gathers the phrases the Qur'an uses elsewhere for that emptiness:

- *"As if they had never lived there"* (11:68)
- *"These are their houses in utter ruin, for they did wrong"* (27:52)
- *"And many a township did We destroy while they were given to wrongdoing, so that it lie in ruins, and (many) a deserted well and lofty castle!"* — part of a longer passage Ibn Kathir cites as (22:45–46)

A deserted well and a high, well-built palace — the ordinary infrastructure of daily life and the proudest architecture a people can raise, both standing there with nobody in them. And the people being addressed are not reading about this in a book. They are walking through it.

**What exactly are the "signs"?** When Allah says *"Verily, therein indeed are signs,"* Ibn Kathir specifies the content: in the fact that these people are gone and have been destroyed, in what happened to them because they disbelieved the Messengers, **and in how those who believed in the Messengers were saved** — in all of that there are many signs, proofs and important lessons. That last piece matters. The lesson of the ruins is not only a threat; it is also a record of rescue. The same history that buried the deniers preserved the believers. Read properly, a ruined city is an argument for faith, not merely a warning against rejection.

**"Would they not then listen?"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this precisely: listen *to the stories of those who came before and what happened to them.* The sign of ayah 26 is a sign that reaches a person through the ear. It is history, testimony, narrative. You receive it by attending to what happened to other people — which is exactly the kind of knowledge a proud person refuses, because it requires admitting that someone else's fate could be his own.

## Where the blindness actually sits

The passage Ibn Kathir cites here does not stop at the ruined township. He carries it on — *"Have they not travelled through the land …"* — until the words that diagnose the whole problem: *"but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind"* (22:45–46).

This is the key to the passage. The eyes of these people work. Their ears work. They walk through the ruins and they look at the crops. The organ that has failed is the heart in the breast. So when the two ayat ask "will they not listen?" and "will they not see?", the questions are not about sensory ability at all — they are about the capacity to be affected, to draw a conclusion, to let evidence change you. A person can stand in the graveyard of a civilisation and register nothing beyond the quality of the light.

## Ayah 27: water driven to ground that cannot ask for it

The second sign is drawn from the opposite end of experience. Not death but life; not something long ago but something this season.

**"The dry land."** The Arabic word is *al-juruz*. Ibn Kathir defines it as the land where nothing grows, and points to the same word in 18:8 — *"And verily, We shall make all that is on it a bare dry soil"* — barren land where nothing grows. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same sense: barren land where trees do not grow. Hold that picture: not merely thirsty ground, but ground with no vegetative future of its own.

**"We drive water."** Ibn Kathir reads this as an explanation of Allah's kindness and goodness towards these very people who deny Him: He sends them water, whether from the sky or as water flowing through the land, water carried by rivers down from the mountains to the lands that need it — and he adds, *at particular times*. Not water in general, but water arriving where it is needed, when it is needed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices something easy to walk past, and it is the most striking observation in the passage. **Usually the Qur'an describes the greening of dry land by saying that the land receives rain, so that it becomes moist and growth-worthy. But there is no mention of rain in this ayah at all.** Instead, the water itself is said to be directed to move along the ground towards the dry land. That is: the rain is made to fall on some other land, and from there the water is directed to travel in the form of carrier channels across the ground, all the way to a dry land that receives no rain of its own.

**The hint embedded in that choice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why this arrangement is a mercy and not merely a mechanism: some lands are so soft that they cannot withstand rains. If regular rains fell on them, buildings might collapse or trees be uprooted. So the rain is sent instead onto land capable of holding it, and the water is then made to flow from there to the lands that could not have withstood the rains — like the land of Egypt. Some commentators pointed to certain lands of Yaman and Syria as intended by this ayah; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this as reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan. Its own conclusion is that the subject includes all such lands, with Egypt — known for its scanty rains — particularly in view: water from the rains in the Abyssinian territory of Africa comes into Egypt through the Nile, bringing with it particles of the indigenous red soil that is good for the growth of crops. So the people of Egypt, though no rains fall in their country, benefit from a supply of **new water and new soil every year**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the thought with the Qur'an's own words: *"So, glorious is Allah, the Best of creators"* (23:14).

Sit with that as an argument. A country is fed by rainfall in another country. The water is delivered, the fertile soil is delivered with it, both by a river, on an annual schedule, to ground that would otherwise be barren — and to people whom the rains would have ruined had they been sent directly. Every element of that is a decision. To eat that bread and conclude that nobody arranged this is not caution; it is a refusal to read.

**"Providing food for their cattle and themselves."** The ayah names the animals' food alongside their own. The provision does not stop at the human beings being argued with; it feeds the livestock they live off. Ibn Kathir pairs the ayah with: *"Then let man look at his food: We pour forth water in abundance"* (80:24–25). The invitation is startlingly ordinary — look at your lunch and trace it backwards.

## Why these two signs stand side by side

Ibn Kathir heads his comment on ayah 27: *the revival of the earth with water is proof of the Resurrection to come.* That is the thread running under both ayat, and it explains why they belong together.

Ayah 26 shows populated cities turned into empty ground. Ayah 27 shows empty ground turned into growing crops. The One who emptied the first can fill the second; the One who brings a harvest out of land where nothing grows can bring people out of the earth that swallowed those nations. Those who deny the Resurrection are being shown both halves of the process, in the landscape they live in, on foot.

And the two signs recruit the two different ways a human being takes in evidence. The ruins are *heard* — you learn them as reports, stories, history. The harvest is *seen* — you learn it with your own eyes, this year, in your own fields. Between hearing and seeing there is no third route by which a claim could reach a person. The passage closes off both exits and leaves the question standing: if not this, then what were you waiting for?

## What the passage asks of a believer

**Treat history as evidence, not entertainment.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on *"would they not then listen"* — listen to the stories of those who came before and what happened to them — makes attention to the fate of earlier peoples a religious act. And read the whole record: the destruction of those who rejected the Messengers *and* the salvation of those who believed in them.

**Let ordinary provision work as an argument, not settle into habit.** Rain that fell somewhere else, a river that arrived on time, soil delivered along with the water, food on the plate. 80:24–25 makes the reflection concrete: look at your food. What the passage indicts is not ignorance of these facts but familiarity with them.

**Suspect the heart before the evidence.** The words Ibn Kathir carries in from 22:45–46 locate the blindness in the heart within the breast, not in the eye. When a sign leaves us unmoved, the honest first question is not what is missing in the sign.

Both ayat end in a question rather than a verdict, and that is itself a mercy. The ruins are still standing, the crops still come up, and the hearing and the sight are still working. Nothing in the passage says the case is closed — only that the evidence has been delivered, twice, and is waiting for someone to read it.

passages.title: When is the Day of Decision?
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrah as-Sajdah with an exchange: the deniers throw a taunting question at the Prophet ﷺ — *when* is this promised decision? — Allah answers it, and then tells His Messenger how to carry himself until the answer arrives. What holds the passage together is one word, **al-fatḥ**, "the Decision": the disbelievers use it as a joke, Allah takes it back from them and turns it into a warning, and ayah 30 leaves both parties standing in the same posture — waiting — for opposite outcomes.

## The taunt behind ayah 28

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 28 as the disbelievers **trying to hurry the punishment along** — actively inviting Allah's wrath and vengeance upon themselves, because they thought this punishment would never happen, and because of their disbelief and stubbornness.

He puts their words into plain speech: *"When will you prevail over us, O Muhammad? You claim there will come a time when you gain the upper hand over us and take your revenge on us — so when will that happen? All we see of you and your companions is that you are hiding, afraid and humiliated."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same picture from ayah 28: what they are asking about is the **victory of the believers against the disbelievers that the Prophet ﷺ had promised**, and they are wondering about it because they see no traces of any such likelihood anywhere around them. Instead they see the Muslims as a group of people, scared and hiding.

This is worth sitting with, because it tells you what kind of question ayah 28 is. It is not a sincere request for a date. It is the confidence of people reading the visible balance of power and concluding that the promise is empty. Their closing clause — *"if you are truthful"* — is the sneer inside the sentence: they are not asking *when*, they are saying *never*.

## What "al-fatḥ" actually means here

Everything in the passage hinges on this word, and the two commentaries handle it with real care.

In ordinary usage, *fatḥ* is what the mockers heard: opening, breakthrough, **victory** — the triumph the Prophet ﷺ had promised. That is exactly the sense Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says they had in mind.

Ibn Kathir's stated position is that what is meant by *al-fatḥ* here is **Judgement** — and he supports that reading not by assertion but by pointing to the Qur'an's own use of this root, where it carries the sense of judging and deciding:

- Nūḥ's words to his Lord: *"So **aftaḥ** (judge) between me and them"* (26:118).
- *"Say: Our Lord will assemble us all together, then He will judge (**yaftaḥu**) between us with truth"* (34:26).
- *"And they sought judgement (**wa-staftaḥū**), and every obstinate, arrogant dictator was brought to a complete loss and destruction"* (14:15).
- *"...although aforetime they had invoked Allah to pass judgement (**yastaftiḥūn**) over those who disbelieved"* (2:89).
- *"If you ask for a judgement (**in tastaftiḥū**), now has the judgement (**al-fatḥ**) come unto you"* (8:19).

So the word the mockers used as a boast about worldly fortunes is, in Allah's answer, the language of a verdict. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that translating *al-fatḥ* as "decision" is deliberate: that rendering admits both probabilities the commentators discussed.

## Ibn Kathir's argument that this is not the conquest of Makkah

Some commentators took *al-fatḥ* in ayah 29 to be the conquest of Makkah. Ibn Kathir rejects this in unusually strong terms — he says those who claim it **"go too far, and have made a grievous mistake"** — and his reasoning is a piece of clear evidence-based argument worth following:

Ayah 29 says that on the Day of al-Fatḥ **the faith of the disbelievers will not benefit them**. But on the day of the conquest of Makkah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ *accepted* the Islam of the freed Makkan prisoners-of-war, who numbered nearly two thousand. If what was meant by this ayah was the conquest of Makkah, he would not have accepted their Islam — because the ayah states plainly that faith offered on that Day brings no profit.

The Prophet's ﷺ own conduct on the day of the conquest, in other words, rules out that reading. The Day spoken of in ayah 29 must therefore be a Day on which the door of belief has closed — which points to judgement, not to a military victory that opened its arms to thousands of new Muslims.

## When is that Day? The views, and what they share

The sources do not flatten this into one answer, and neither should we.

**Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 29** — *"Say: On the Day of al-Fatḥ..."* — is: *"when the wrath and punishment of Allah befall you, in this world and the next."* So for him the Day of Decision is the descent of Allah's judgement, whether that lands in this life or the next.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān**, drawing on Ibn Kathir, spells the same thing out as a reply to the taunt: *why are you asking us about the day of our victory, while that day is going to be a day of trouble for you?* When victory comes to the believers, the mockers will already have been overtaken by punishment — maybe **right here in this world, as it happened in the Battle of Badr** — or else in the Hereafter. And when the punishment of Allah seizes someone, no profession of faith at that time, no declaration of *īmān* at that stage, is accepted.

**A second view** is reported honestly by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: there are others who have interpreted the "day" in *"When will this decision take place?"* (ayah 28) as **the day of Qiyāmah** — the Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the summarised explanation of this verse in *Bayān-ul-Qurʼān*, appearing in the original edition of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself, is based on that tafsir, and that translating *al-fatḥ* as "decision" admits both probabilities.

What both readings agree on is the point that actually matters to the reader: there is a Day on which the matter is decided — and once Allah's punishment arrives, faith offered then is not accepted.

## "Nor will they be granted a respite" — why late faith is not faith

The second half of ayah 29 has two clauses, and they close two different escape routes.

*"Their faith will not benefit them"* — the door of belief shuts. Ibn Kathir says this is like the ayah: *"Then when their Messengers came to them with clear proofs, they were glad with that which they had of the knowledge..."* (40:83).

*"Nor will they be granted a respite"* — the door of delay shuts too. There is no extra time, no adjournment to think it over.

Put together, the ayah exposes what the mocking question in ayah 28 really was: a bet that there would always be time. Faith is only faith while it is a free response to an unseen promise. Once the punishment is visibly at the door, "believing" is no longer belief — it is simply seeing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrasing is stark: when the punishment of Allah seizes someone, the declaration of *īmān* **at that stage** is not accepted.

## Ayah 30: what the Prophet ﷺ is told to do meanwhile

*"So turn away from them, and wait! They too are waiting."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the command in two movements. **Turn away** means: *turn away from these idolaters, and convey that which has been revealed to you from your Lord.* Note that this is not withdrawal from the mission — it is disengagement from the argument so that the mission can continue. He links it to *"Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord — there is no deity but Him"* (6:106). The taunt does not deserve a debate; it deserves to be left behind while the revelation is delivered.

**And wait** means: *wait until Allah fulfils that which He has promised you, and grants you victory over those who oppose you* — and Ibn Kathir adds the ground of that waiting: **He never breaks His promise.** The waiting commanded here is not passivity or uncertainty; it is confidence with a delay in it.

## Two kinds of waiting

The most striking thing in ayah 30 is that the same verb is turned on both parties. *Wa-ntaẓir* — "and wait," to the Prophet ﷺ. *Innahum muntaẓirūn* — "they too are waiting." Ibn Kathir's gloss: *you are waiting, and they are waiting and plotting against you.*

For what were they waiting? He answers with another ayah that preserves their own voice: *"Or do they say: A poet! We await for him some calamity by time!"* (52:30) — waiting for time itself to take him.

So the sūrah ends with two parties in an identical posture and opposite expectations. Ibn Kathir closes the sūrah on the outcome: *you will see the consequences of your patience towards them, and the fulfilment of the promise of your Lord in your victory over them; and they will see the consequences of their wait for something bad to befall you and your Companions, in that Allah's punishment will come upon them.* He then adds the words of trust with which he ends this sūrah's commentary: **"Sufficient unto us is Allah, and He is the Best Disposer of affairs."**

## Living it

**Do not measure a promise by the present balance of power.** Ayah 28 is a taunt built entirely on appearances — a frightened group in hiding, no trace of victory anywhere in sight. The appearances were accurate. The conclusion drawn from them was wrong. What looks decisive today is not the verdict.

**Learn the two responses to mockery from ayah 30.** Turn away — and keep conveying what was revealed to you. Ibn Kathir's reading refuses both extremes: you neither trade insults with the mocker nor go quiet about the truth. You disengage from the quarrel and get on with the message.

**Understand what kind of "waiting" you are asked for.** It is not resignation. It rests on a specific conviction Ibn Kathir names: Allah never breaks His promise. The believer's waiting is the confidence of someone who knows the verdict is coming.

**Take the warning in ayah 29 personally, not only historically.** The mockers assumed there would be room to change their minds later. The ayah answers that there will be no benefit in faith then and no respite granted. That is a warning about postponement itself — about treating repentance and turning back to Allah as something available at some vague later point. Ibn Kathir tells us the word *al-fatḥ* here means Judgement; the time to set your account right is before the judgement falls.
